title: Ask Team Members to Create Their Own Goals
author: Admired Leadership Field Notes
summary: Most leaders design goals and hand them down because they do not trust team members to craft goals that stretch performance. The result is a goal set the team member never internalizes. Flip the workflow: ask team members to draft initial goals, use the draft to open dialogue, and co-create the final version. The three-type taxonomy replaces outcome-only lists. Outcome goals are measurable end states heavily influenced by external factors. Performance goals are big actions within the team member's control that produce outcomes. Process goals are specific behaviors and skills that drive performance. All three are required. Outcomes alone leave the team member guessing what to do. Process and performance alone lack a destination. The combination gives leader and team member multiple timescales for measuring progress, so feedback does not wait for quarterly outcomes. The posture is direct: ask team members for a tight draft across all three types, then negotiate the final set together.
points: Most leaders design goals and hand them down without input, producing goal sets team members never internalize.

Three types of goals are required: Outcome (measurable end states), Performance (big actions under team control that produce outcomes), and Process (specific behaviors and skills driving performance).
Outcomes alone leave team members guessing what to do; process and performance alone leave them without a destination; all three together enable multiple timescales for feedback.
Ask team members for a draft across all three types, then co-create the final set; this activates their input and builds commitment.
quotes: Setting individual goals to be achieved in the next calendar year sets expectations for team members and keeps them centered on their personal performance and development. Goals are the lifeblood for enhanced performance, and good leaders use them to measure progress.

The best goal set stretches team members and pushes them to expand their skills and results. A well-crafted set of goals asks a team member to think beyond what they do now and to make significant progress on issues and outcomes that matter.

Unfortunately, too many leaders design, propose, and direct team members by setting goals without their input. They do not trust team members to create the kind of goals that will make a difference in results and performance. As a result, the goal set they create is rarely internalized by team members, nor does it hit all the right notes for true improvement.

The best leaders ask team members to craft their own goal set with an eye toward three distinct goals. They use what team members propose to begin a dialogue around what it will take to elevate performance. They co-create the final goal set to achieve a higher commitment and focus.

Outcome goals, as the name implies, are the results team members want to attain. These are the most common goals identified in planning sessions. They are typically measurable and time-bound, which makes it easy to tell whether they have been achieved or not.

In contrast, performance goals are the big actions that lead to outcomes but are within the control of the team member. They typically focus on a standard of performance or how team members will achieve the outcomes they desire.

Process goals are the specific actions and skills that give rise to performance. Think steps or behaviors that contribute to progress, making performance and results possible. Unlike outcome goals that focus on the end result, process goals focus on the journey and the controllable activities that get people there.

People require all three goal types to make significant progress, whether they are athletes, artists, or team members. Without all three goal types, people often fail to make the strides they should.” Archived from Admired Leadership on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
